claim: Complex scene perception depends upon the interaction between signals from the classical receptive field (CRF) and the extra-classical receptive field (eCRF) in primary visual cortex (V1) neurons.
source: Complex scene perception depends upon the interaction between signals from the classical receptive field (CRF) and the extra-classical receptive field (eCRF) in primary visual cortex (V1) neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement about the role of CRF and eCRF in perception, drawing from established scientific understanding.

claim: Three principal eCRF mechanisms were found: tuned-facilitation, untuned-suppression, and tuned-suppression.
source: We probed the spatio-temporal dynamics of eCRF modulation using a reverse correlation paradigm, and found three principal eCRF mechanisms: tuned-facilitation, untuned-suppression, and tuned-suppression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the reverse correlation paradigm described in the manuscript.

claim: Each eCRF mechanism had a distinct timing and spatial profile.
source: Each mechanism had a distinct timing and spatial profile.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental measurements of timing and spatial extent reported in the results.

claim: The timing, orientation-tuning, and strength of eCRF mechanisms had distinct signatures within magnocellular and parvocellular processing streams in the V1 microcircuit.
source: Laminar analysis showed that the timing, orientation-tuning, and strength of eCRF mechanisms had distinct signatures within magnocellular and parvocellular processing streams in the V1 microcircuit.
evidence: This is supported by the laminar analysis data presented in the results section.

claim: The differences in timing and scale of eCRF mechanisms predicted distinct patterns of net modulation.
source: Modeling revealed that the differences in timing and scale of these mechanisms predicted distinct patterns of net modulation, reconciling many previous disparate physiological and psychophysical findings.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: V1 neurons have classical receptive fields (CRF).
source: Many low- to mid-level computations emerge in neuronal response properties in primary visual cortex (V1) where neurons have both classical (CRF; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Angelucci et al., 2002) and extra-classical (eCRF; Allman et al., 1985; Levitt and Lund, 1997; Angelucci et al., 2002) receptive fields.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: V1 neurons have extra-classical receptive fields (eCRF).
source: Many low- to mid-level computations emerge in neuronal response properties in primary visual cortex (V1) where neurons have both classical (CRF; Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Hubel and Wiesel, 1968; Angelucci et al., 2002) and extra-classical (eCRF; Allman et al., 1985; Levitt and Lund, 1997; Angelucci et al., 2002) receptive fields.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The CRF provides the spatio-temporal filtering properties of the neuron.
source: The CRF provides the spatio-temporal filtering properties of the neuron, and consists of regions where stimuli directly evoke spiking activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional role of the CRF based on established knowledge.

claim: The CRF consists of regions where stimuli directly evoke spiking activity.

claim: The eCRF modulates CRF spiking responses.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Layer 4B neurons had a strong correlation with layer 4Cα dynamics.
source: Layer 4B neurons had a strong correlation with layer 4Cα dynamics (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Layer 6 neurons showed a similarly strong correlation with layer 4Cα neurons.
source: Layer 6 neurons showed a similarly strong correlation with layer 4Cα neurons (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Layer 5 neurons showed similar correlations with both layers 4Cα and 4Cβ.
source: By contrast, layer 5 neurons showed similar correlations with both layers 4Cα and 4Cβ (Figure 4J), similar to the mixed results in layer 2/3.
evidence: This is supported by the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The eCRF of a layer 2/3 neuron does not receive mixed input from layers 4Cα and 4Cβ, but rather receives dominant input from either the M or P pathway.
source: This suggests that the eCRF of a layer 2/3 neuron does not receive mixed input from layers 4Cα and 4Cβ, but rather receives dominant input from either the M or P pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution of correlation differences shown in Figure 4L.

claim: The majority of individual neurons in layers 4B and 6 had dynamics that were better matched to layer 4Cα than to 4Cβ.
source: The correlation pattern in layers 4B and 6 was different; there was a clear bias towards positive correlation-difference values, confirming that the majority of individual neurons in layers 4B and 6 (Figure 4M and O) had dynamics that were better matched to layer 4Cα than to 4Cβ.
evidence: This is supported by the distribution of correlation differences shown in Figure 4M and 4O.

claim: Among the eight layer 5 neurons recorded, the correlation difference split between negative and positive values, suggesting possible stream-specific input onto single neurons.
source: Among the eight layer 5 neurons recorded, the correlation difference also split between negative and positive values (Figure 4N), suggesting possible stream-specific input onto single neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the distribution of correlation differences shown in Figure 4N.

claim: The peak orientations for tuned facilitation and tuned suppression were within 20 degrees of each other.
source: For the population, the peak orientations for tuned facilitation and tuned suppression were within 20 degrees of each other (Figure 5D, F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5D and 5F.

claim: Measures of local selectivity for orientation around the peak (bandwidth) were similarly distributed for both facilitation and suppression.
source: Measures of local selectivity for orientation around the peak (bandwidth) were similarly distributed for both facilitation and suppression (Figure 5E, G), although within individual cells, we found only a weak and not statistically significant relationship between the two bandwidths (Figure 5H, Pearson's correlation, r = 0.22, p=0.14).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 5E, 5G, and 5H.

claim: More global measures of selectivity (the response ratio at orthogonal to preferred orientations) showed a moderate relationship between the tuning for facilitation and suppression.
source: More global measures of selectivity (the response ratio at orthogonal to preferred orientations) showed a moderate relationship between the tuning for facilitation and suppression (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.29, p=0.051).
evidence: This is supported by statistical correlation analysis.

claim: The tuned component of eCRF suppression spanned the same range of selectivity and tuning as that of the facilitation elicited from within and near the CRF.
source: Overall, the tuned component of eCRF suppression spanned the same range of selectivity and tuning as that of the facilitation elicited from within and near the CRF, a comparison only made possible by isolating eCRF component mechanisms.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the tuning comparison data.

claim: Changes in stimulus duration have the potential to alter the net observed steady-state eCRF modulation during stimulus presentation.
source: Consequently, a given eCRF stimulus may recruit multiple underlying eCRF mechanisms with distinct signs and spatio-temporal profiles. As such, changes in stimulus duration have the potential to alter the net observed steady-state eCRF modulation during stimulus presentation.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of multiple eCRF mechanisms.

claim: Briefly presented stimuli will increase the relative influence of short latency eCRF mechanisms.
source: Briefly presented stimuli will increase the relative influence of short latency eCRF mechanisms; prolonged stimuli will allow both short- and long-latency eCRF mechanisms to modulate CRF responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of stimulus duration on eCRF modulation.

claim: Prolonged stimuli will allow both short- and long-latency eCRF mechanisms to modulate CRF responses.
source: Briefly presented stimuli will increase the relative influence of short latency eCRF mechanisms; prolonged stimuli will allow both short- and long-latency eCRF mechanisms to modulate CRF responses.
evidence: This is an inference about the effect of stimulus duration on eCRF modulation.

claim: For brief presentations (<40 ms), there was no net eCRF modulation because both eCRF mechanisms had some intrinsic delay.
source: For brief presentations (<40 ms), there was no net eCRF modulation because both eCRF mechanisms had some intrinsic delay (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For intermediate durations (60–120 ms), the model showed net facilitation, because short-latency facilitation was engaged and had greater impact than delayed suppression.
source: For intermediate durations (60–120 ms), the model showed net facilitation, because short-latency facilitation was engaged and had greater impact than delayed suppression.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For longer durations (>200 ms), stronger long-latency suppression dominated, resulting in net suppressive modulation.
source: For longer durations (>200 ms), stronger long-latency suppression dominated, resulting in net suppressive modulation (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Even for a stimulus of fixed orientation in the eCRF, changing stimulus duration altered both the sign and the magnitude of net eCRF modulation.
source: Thus, even for a stimulus of fixed orientation in the eCRF, changing stimulus duration altered both the sign and the magnitude of net eCRF modulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: For stimuli of short-duration, there is no modulation (40–60 ms) in the model with untuned and tuned suppression.
source: For stimuli of short-duration, there is no modulation (40–60 ms) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For stimulus durations of 80–100 ms, the measurable eCRF suppression was largely unselective for orientation in the model with untuned and tuned suppression.
source: For stimulus durations of 80–100 ms, the measurable eCRF suppression was largely unselective for orientation.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For stimulus durations > 200 ms, the response reflected a combination of both orientation-untuned and orientation-tuned mechanisms in the model with untuned and tuned suppression.
source: For stimulus durations > 200 ms, the response reflected a combination of both orientation-untuned and orientation-tuned mechanisms.
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Stimuli of short duration or the integration of spiking activity over windows immediately after stimulus onset will bias net modulation toward component mechanisms that have the shortest latency.
source: In general, however, stimuli of short duration or the integration of spiking activity over windows immediately after stimulus onset will bias net modulation toward component mechanisms that have the shortest latency.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Stimuli of longer duration or integration over time windows that are significantly delayed after stimulus onset will afford more equal contribution by eCRF mechanisms that have diverse temporal dynamics.
source: By contrast, stimuli of longer duration or integration over time windows that are significantly delayed after stimulus onset will afford more equal contribution by eCRF mechanisms that have diverse temporal dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Facilitation occurred early, was spatially localized to regions within and near the CRF, and generally matched the preferred orientation of the CRF.
source: Facilitation occurred early, was spatially localized to regions within and near the CRF, and generally matched the preferred orientation of the CRF.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings on facilitation.

claim: The tuned facilitatory component of eCRF modulation is generated in the compact local circuitry of a few neighboring cortical hypercolumns and, in turn, generates CRF signals.
source: Thus we propose that the tuned facilitatory component of eCRF modulation is generated in the compact local circuitry of a few neighboring cortical hypercolumns and, in turn, generates CRF signals.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: Some studies have reported facilitation from 'far' regions of the eCRF, but generally only when a low contrast stimulus drove the CRF and when stimuli were absent from regions of the 'near' surround.
source: Some studies have reported facilitation from 'far' regions of the eCRF (Schwabe et al., 2006; Ichida et al., 2007), but generally only when a low contrast stimulus drove the CRF and when stimuli were absent from regions of the 'near' surround.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In the current study, there was always a stimulus covering the near surround, which might explain the lack of facilitation at the largest spatial extents.
source: In our study, there was always a stimulus covering the near surround, which might explain the lack of facilitation at the largest spatial extents.
evidence: This is an inference about why the current results differ from some prior studies.

claim: Earlier studies that reported strong facilitation found facilitation only from flanking stimuli that were relatively close to the CRF.
source: By contrast, earlier studies that reported strong facilitation (Kapadia et al., 1995; Polat et al., 1998; Kapadia et al., 2000) found facilitation only from flanking stimuli that were relatively close to the CRF.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The facilitation reported in earlier studies is consistent with the spatiotemporal scale of facilitation observed in the current study and localized to extensions of a central CRF mechanism.
source: This facilitation is consistent with the spatiotemporal scale of facilitation that we observed and have localized to extensions of a central CRF mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current findings to prior work.

claim: Stimuli in earlier studies were often presented over fairly brief durations, which as the modeling results illustrate will bias net modulation towards the shortest-latency facilitation component.
source: Further, stimuli in these studies were often presented over fairly brief durations, which as our modeling results illustrate will bias net modulation towards this shortest-latency facilitation component.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the modeling results to prior work.

claim: There was a pronounced facilitation at the orthogonal-to-preferred orientation in the average layer 5 eCRF dynamics.
source: There was a pronounced facilitation at the orthogonal-to-preferred orientation in the average layer 5 eCRF dynamics (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Orthogonal eCRF facilitation was also seen, although with a reduced amplitude, in the dynamics from layers 4B, 4C and 6.
source: This was also seen, although with a reduced amplitude, in the dynamics from layers 4B, 4C and 6 (Figure 4B,D,F).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B, 4D, and 4F.

claim: Earlier studies reported examples of orthogonal eCRF facilitation but the layers of the recorded neurons were not reported.
source: Earlier studies reported examples of orthogonal eCRF facilitation (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Jones et al., 2002) but the layers of the recorded neurons were not reported.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The peak time of facilitation at the preferred orientation was 25–50 ms earlier than orthogonal facilitation for the layer 5 kernels, suggesting that different circuits contributed to these two components.
source: The peak time of facilitation at the preferred orientation was 25–50 ms earlier than orthogonal facilitation for the layer 5 kernels (Figure 4E), suggesting that different circuits contributed to these two components.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the timing differences shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The untuned component of eCRF suppression arose early and was associated with V1 layers receiving or relaying LGN-magnocellular input.
source: We found that the untuned component of eCRF suppression arose early and was associated with V1 layers receiving or relaying LGN-magnocellular input.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings on untuned suppression.

claim: A proportion of V1 untuned suppression may arise from subcortical eCRF suppression.
source: This suggests that a proportion of V1 untuned suppression may arise from subcortical eCRF suppression (Webb et al., 2005), which has been found in magnocellular–projecting retinal ganglion cells (Solomon et al., 2006) and in magnocellular LGN cells (Solomon et al., 2002; Sceniak et al., 2006; Alitto and Usrey, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to prior work on subcortical suppression.

claim: The short latency, limited spatial scale, and lack of orientation tuning of untuned suppression are consistent with the idea that it derives from feedforward magnocellular LGN input.
source: The short latency, limited spatial scale, and lack of orientation tuning of this component of suppression are consistent with the idea that it derives from feedforward magnocellular LGN input.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the properties of untuned suppression.

claim: Some untuned suppression may arise from local, lateral cortico-cortical inhibition.
source: However, our results suggest that some untuned suppression may arise from local, lateral cortico-cortical inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial extent and timing data.

claim: Although untuned suppression was reduced in strength at distances beyond 2x eCRF border, it was not zero at this larger spatial scale.
source: Although we found that untuned suppression was reduced in strength at distances beyond 2x eCRF border, it was not zero at this larger spatial scale.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial extent of untuned suppression.

claim: Broad distributions in the strength and time to peak of untuned suppression suggest additional cortical processing beyond common inherited effects from the LGN.
source: Broad distributions in the strength and time to peak of this untuned suppression (Figure 2) also suggest additional cortical processing beyond common inherited effects from the LGN.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability in untuned suppression properties.

claim: Untuned suppression was also observed in individual neurons in the parvocellular input layer 4Cβ and in layers 2/3 with a delay of 100 ms or more.
source: Although untuned suppression was most prevalent in layer 4B, it was also observed in individual neurons in the parvocellular input layer 4Cβ and in layers 2/3 (although it was lost in the average of layer 2/3) and it was found with a delay of 100 ms or more.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the presence of delayed untuned suppression in parvocellular layers.

claim: Delayed component of untuned suppression in neurons with parvocellular-dominated input is likely to be cortically generated, because eCRF suppression is not observed in parvocellular LGN cells.
source: This delayed component of untuned suppression in neurons with parvocellular-dominated input is likely to be cortically generated, because eCRF suppression is not observed in parvocellular LGN cells (Alitto and Usrey, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Untuned suppression may result from multiple processes, including suppression in magnocellular LGN feedforward input as well as lateral cortico-cortical inhibition.
source: Together, the evidence suggests that untuned suppression may result from multiple processes, including suppression in magnocellular LGN feedforward input as well as lateral cortico-cortical inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined evidence on untuned suppression.

claim: In a previous study using steady state stimulation, some neurons in layers 2/3 showed eCRF suppression components that had high contrast sensitivities, indicative of M-pathway involvement.
source: In a previous study, using steady state stimulation (Henry et al., 2013), we reported that for some neurons, the eCRF suppression in layers 2/3 showed components that had high contrast sensitivities, indicative of M-pathway involvement.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: In the previous study, the suppression was strong at both collinear and orthogonal eCRF orientations, indicating that the untuned component was contributing.
source: Furthermore, the suppression was strong at both collinear and orthogonal eCRF orientations, indicating that the untuned component was contributing.
evidence: This is a statement about findings from a prior study by the authors.

claim: The main early component of eCRF suppression is untuned and attributed to the M-pathway, which has characteristically high contrast sensitivity.
source: In the current results, the main early component is also untuned and we attribute this to the M-pathway, which has characteristically high contrast sensitivity (Kaplan and Shapley, 1986).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work on M-pathway properties.

claim: The untuned component of eCRF suppression may be predominantly derived from magnocellular signals relayed by 4Cα neurons to neurons in other V1 layers.
source: These results refine the view that there are both tuned and untuned components of the eCRF (Henry et al., 2013; Nurminen and Angelucci, 2014); the untuned component of eCRF suppression may be predominantly derived from magnocellular signals relayed by 4Cα neurons to neurons in other V1 layers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the laminar analysis and supported by citations.

claim: A recent study on timing of eCRF effects between layers did not appear to show strong M- and P-pathway separation.
source: A recent study on timing of eCRF effects between layers did not appear to show strong M- and P-pathway separation (Bijanzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: It is difficult to compare the results of the current study with those of the Bijanzadeh et al. study, which recorded LFP and MUA using a fixed size of CRF and eCRF stimuli.
source: However, it is difficult to compare the results of our current study with those of the Bijanzadeh et al. study, which recorded LFP and MUA using a fixed size of CRF and eCRF stimuli, because probing for local untuned suppression depends on measuring the border between the CRF and eCRF, which may differ for individual neurons.
evidence: This is an explanation for why the current results may differ from a prior study.

claim: Tuned suppression was observed in both input layers and very prominently in layer 2/3.
source: Tuned suppression was observed in both input layers and very prominently in layer 2/3.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings on tuned suppression.

claim: Layer 2/3 suppression peaked at times that were quite delayed compared to those at which facilitation occurred.
source: Layer 2/3 suppression peaked at times that were quite delayed compared to those at which facilitation occurred.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the timing of suppression in layer 2/3.

claim: Both the orientation selectivity and the delayed emergence of tuned suppression are consistent with its arising as a result of cortico-cortical lateral interactions.
source: Both the orientation selectivity and the delayed emergence of this tuned suppression are consistent with its arising as a result of cortico-cortical lateral interactions, as often postulated before (reviewed in Angelucci et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: The tuned suppressive component arises from extended spatial scales, with most of it generated by the activity of V1 neurons with receptive fields more than 2 x the CRF radius away from the recorded neuron.
source: We found that this suppressive component arises from extended spatial scales, with most of it generated by the activity of V1 neurons with receptive fields more than 2 x the CRF radius away from the recorded neuron.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the spatial extent of tuned suppression.

claim: Long-distance V1 lateral connections must be in some way selective for the orientation of their targets in order to support such long-range tuned suppression.
source: Long-distance V1 lateral connections must be in some way selective for the orientation of their targets in order to support such long-range tuned suppression (Malach et al., 1993).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to prior work on lateral connections.

claim: If tuned suppression is caused in part by extra-striate feedback, then those feedback circuits must also be matched in orientation selectivity to their V1 targets.
source: If instead this suppression is caused in part by extra-striate feedback (Angelucci et al., 2002; Angelucci et al., 2017; Nassi et al., 2013), then those feedback circuits must also be matched in orientation selectivity to their V1 targets.
evidence: This is a conditional inference supported by citations to prior work on feedback.

claim: Tuned suppression is also present in layer 4B, where it differs quantitatively from that of layers 2/3.
source: Tuned suppression is also present in layer 4B, where it differs quantitatively from that of layers 2/3.
evidence: This is a direct statement about tuned suppression in layer 4B.

claim: In layer 4B, tuned suppression is very rapid, and its presence is partially obscured because it overlaps to some extent with untuned suppression.
source: In layer 4B, tuned suppression is very rapid, and its presence is partially obscured because it overlaps to some extent with untuned suppression (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the properties of tuned suppression in layer 4B, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: A small sample of layer 4B cells (n = 6) probed using eCRF stimuli with an inner radius of 2x eCRF border showed strong early tuned suppression.
source: We examined a small sample of layer 4B cells (n = 6) probed using eCRF stimuli with an inner radius of 2x eCRF border, a scale at which the early untuned suppression is no longer present, and found strong early tuned suppression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings in a subset of layer 4B cells, supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: These results point towards a fast, tuned-suppression mechanism that is specific to layer 4B, distinct from that seen in layers 2/3.
source: These results point towards a fast, tuned-suppression mechanism that is specific to layer 4B, distinct from that seen in layers 2/3.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the layer 4B data.

claim: Tuned suppression may be elaborated via multiple circuit mechanisms along distinct cortico-cortical output pathways.
source: These results imply that tuned suppression may also be elaborated via multiple circuit mechanisms along distinct cortico-cortical output pathways.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differences in tuned suppression across layers.

claim: The orientation selectivity of the tuned component of eCRF suppression was similar to that of facilitation arising from regions near the CRF.
source: We found that the orientation selectivity of the tuned component of eCRF suppression was similar to that of facilitation arising from regions near the CRF.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the comparison of orientation selectivity.

claim: Earlier studies concluded that the tuning of eCRF suppression was broader than that of the CRF.
source: Yet earlier studies concluded that the tuning of eCRF suppression was broader than that of the CRF (Webb et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Earlier inferences about broader tuning of eCRF suppression were based on steady-state responses that included both the untuned and tuned components of eCRF suppression and did not discriminate between them.
source: However, these inferences were based on steady-state responses that included both the untuned and tuned components of eCRF suppression and did not discriminate between them.
evidence: This is an explanation for why earlier studies reached different conclusions.

claim: During prolonged visual stimulation with extended patterns, steady-state measurements of eCRF modulation incorporate both facilitatory and suppressive eCRF mechanisms.
source: During prolonged visual stimulation with extended patterns, steady-state measurements of eCRF modulation incorporate both facilitatory and suppressive eCRF mechanisms, because their response dynamics are fast compared to stimulus presentation times.
evidence: This is an inference about how steady-state measurements integrate multiple mechanisms.

claim: In the modeling responses to stimuli with shorter presentation durations, the relative contributions of facilitation and suppression mechanisms depended on stimulus presentation time.
source: In the modeling responses to stimuli with shorter presentation durations, as often used in psychophysical studies, the relative contributions of these mechanisms depended on stimulus presentation time (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: The new results help to reconcile the seemingly contradictory results in the literature.
source: These new results help to reconcile the seemingly contradictory results in the literature.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the current findings.

claim: Studies using large collinear annular gratings drifting for hundreds of milliseconds to many seconds typically reported strong eCRF collinear suppression but little or no collinear facilitation.
source: Studies of eCRF modulation that used large collinear annular gratings drifting for hundreds of milliseconds to many seconds typically reported strong eCRF collinear suppression but little or no collinear facilitation (Levitt and Lund, 1997; Hupé et al., 2001; Sceniak et al., 2001; Levitt and Lund, 2002; Cavanaugh et al., 2002a; Jones et al., 2002; Shushruth et al., 2012; Nassi et al., 2013; Henry et al., 2013; Trott and Born, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Other studies that used briefly presented spatially localized stimuli flanking the CRF reported a high prevalence of collinear facilitation.
source: Other studies that used briefly presented spatially localized stimuli flanking the CRF (Kapadia et al., 1995; Kapadia et al., 2000) reported a high prevalence of collinear facilitation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: In the current study, both types of responses (facilitation and suppression) were observed.
source: In the current study, we observed both types of responses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the findings of the current study.

claim: Early facilitation from the defined eCRF border was observed in about 25% of neurons.
source: We found an early facilitation from the defined eCRF border in about 25% of neurons.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the prevalence of facilitation.

claim: Most neurons that showed an early facilitation possessed tuned suppression that was temporally delayed.
source: Most neurons that showed an early facilitation possessed tuned suppression that was temporally delayed (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the co-occurrence of facilitation and suppression, supported by Figure 3E.

claim: With a biphasic temporal profile, integration of the spiking response over short epochs yields facilitation when compared to CRF stimulation alone.
source: With this biphasic temporal profile, integration of the spiking response over short epochs yields facilitation when compared to CRF stimulation alone (Figure 6), as observed by Kapadia et al., 2000.
evidence: This is an inference supported by the modeling results in Figure 6 and a citation to prior work.

claim: Integration of the response over longer stimulus durations leads to net measured suppression as the stronger, delayed suppressive component dominates over facilitation.
source: Integration of the response over longer stimulus durations leads to net measured suppression as the stronger, delayed suppressive component dominates over facilitation (Figure 6), as reported in many studies (Jones et al., 2001; Sceniak et al., 2001; Cavanaugh et al., 2002b; Webb et al., 2005; Hallum and Movshon, 2014; Trott and Born, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference supported by the modeling results in Figure 6 and citations to prior work.

claim: Differences in temporal integration among multiple eCRF components provide a parsimonious explanation for many previous conflicting reports about eCRF facilitation.
source: We suggest that these differences in temporal integration among multiple eCRF components provide a parsimonious explanation for many previous conflicting reports about eCRF facilitation (and lack thereof).
evidence: This is an inference about how the current findings reconcile prior conflicting results.

claim: It has been increasingly argued that normalization represents a 'canonical computation' in neuronal circuits.
source: Through recent work, it has been increasingly argued that normalization represents a 'canonical computation' in neuronal circuits, a computational motif that is repeated in each cortical area to adjust individual neuronal responses on the basis of the average population activity (Carandini and Heeger, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Normalization models have proved a useful quantitative framework for characterizing spatial nonlinearities in neuronal responses.
source: Normalization models have proved a useful quantitative framework for characterizing spatial nonlinearities in neuronal responses, ranging from contrast gain control in retinal ganglion cells (Shapley and Victor, 1979) to cross-orientation suppression within V1 CRFs (Carandini et al., 1997) and V1 eCRF modulation (Cavanaugh et al., 2002a; Cavanaugh et al., 2002b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on normalization models.

claim: Often the assumption is that all neurons within a given cortical area possess the same response gating from a single normalization process.
source: Some studies dissect normalization into equivalent specific mechanistic classes, such as 'tuned' normalization (Verhoef and Maunsell, 2017; Ni and Maunsell, 2017), but often the assumption is that all neurons within a given cortical area possess the same response gating from a single normalization process.
evidence: This is a statement about a common assumption in the field, supported by citations.

claim: There are clear differences at the microcircuit level in the scale, tuning and timing of recruited normalization processes in V1.
source: As our results in V1 highlight, there are clear differences at the microcircuit level in the scale, tuning and timing of recruited normalization processes.
evidence: This is a summary of the implications of the current findings.

claim: Diversity across neurons in normalization is partially explained by laminar differences in overall connectivity with the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways in the cortical input layer.
source: This diversity across neurons is partially explained by laminar differences in overall connectivity with the magnocellular and parvocellular pathways in the cortical input layer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the laminar analysis.

claim: The 'tuned' normalization observed in the V1 output layers shows clear distinctions in timing between layers 2/3 and layer 4B, suggesting the existence of further elaborated and segregated microcircuits.
source: However, even the 'tuned' normalization that we observe in the V1 output layers shows clear distinctions in timing between layers 2/3 and layer 4B, suggesting the existence of further elaborated and segregated microcircuits.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the laminar differences in tuned suppression.

claim: Normalization has been proposed as a computation that serves to adjust neurons' responses to span a non-saturating operating range.
source: Normalization has been proposed as a computation that serves to adjust neurons' responses to span a non-saturating operating range (Ringach, 2010) and to reduce redundancy across the population (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on the function of normalization.

claim: Normalization has been proposed as a computation that serves to reduce redundancy across the population.
source: Normalization has been proposed as a computation that serves to adjust neurons' responses to span a non-saturating operating range (Ringach, 2010) and to reduce redundancy across the population (Schwartz and Simoncelli, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work on the function of normalization.

claim: It is incorrect to equate one cortical area with one canonical normalization process common to all neurons.
source: Within this framework, our results suggest that it is incorrect to equate one cortical area with one canonical normalization process common to all neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the diversity of normalization mechanisms observed.

claim: It may prove more fruitful to dissect the cortical circuit into functional modules based on their downstream targets and to ask what consequences specific normalization mechanisms have for signaling in broader recurrent circuits.
source: Instead, it may prove more fruitful to dissect the cortical circuit into functional modules based on their downstream targets and to ask what consequences specific normalization mechanisms have for signaling in broader recurrent circuits.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research based on the current findings.

claim: Diversity in normalization has been shown to underlie the generation of increasing RF selectivity.
source: In part, this diversity in normalization has been shown to underlie the generation of increasing RF selectivity (Xing et al., 2005; Xing et al., 2011), resulting in distinct spatiotemporal transformations from the input layer to the various cortical output pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The findings of multiple component mechanisms of eCRF modulation that have different dynamics lead to interesting predictions for visual perception.
source: These findings of multiple component mechanisms of eCRF modulation that have different dynamics lead to interesting predictions for visual perception.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Extended stimuli with varied spatial structure will differentially affect the coding of localized stimuli.
source: They predict that extended stimuli with varied spatial structure will differentially affect the coding of localized stimuli, a phenomenon that is well-characterized in perceptual studies of meta-contrast masking (Ishikawa et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a prediction supported by a citation to prior work on masking.

claim: Stimuli of identical spatial structure may influence perception differently, depending on the time frame over which they are viewed.
source: Further, they predict that stimuli of identical spatial structure may influence perception differently, depending on the time frame over which they are viewed.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the findings of temporal dynamics.

claim: A study that measured discrimination by human and rodent subjects of a central grating patch in the presence of a surrounding patch reported different outcomes between the two species.
